readerTitle: The deal you lost knows something you don't
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장 상자 제조사, 병원 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 상황과 수치는 설명용
insight: 잃은 거래의 '공식 이유'는 대개 예의 바른 작별 인사다. 진짜 이유는 고객이 대신 무엇을 골랐고 어디서 마음이 바뀌었는지에 있다.
misconception: 고객이 '가격이 비싸서'라고 하면 가격 문제다. 진 거래는 빨리 잊고 다음 거래로 넘어가는 게 낫다.

sources.text: 영업 실무의 일반적 방법 (win-loss review, 실패 거래 회고)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 수치(가격 차이 약 4%, 리드타임 3주 대 1주, 체험 5건 중 3건 실패)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 특정 연구나 통계를 인용하지 않았습니다.
'고객이 밝힌 이유가 진짜 이유와 다른 경우가 많다'는 점은 영업 실무에서 널리 쓰이는 관찰로만 서술했습니다. 비율 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과장되지 않았는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The deal you lost knows something you don't
body: Dana runs a small factory that makes custom shipping boxes. She spent six weeks courting a regional distributor. Samples, site visits, a sharp quote.
Then a one-line email: "We've decided to go another way. Your price was a bit high."
Most founders read that line, sigh, and move on. That line is where the useful part begins.

image.label: A founder reading a short rejection email beside a stack of boxes
image.brief: 작은 공장 사무실. 골판지 상자 샘플이 쌓인 책상 앞에서 창업자가 노트북 속 한 줄짜리 이메일을 보고 있음. 이메일 문구 일부 "...your price was a bit high." 보이게. 실제 회사 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: "Your price was a bit high." What now?
body: Dana has three more bids going out this month. She has limited time and no sales team.
What should she do with this lost deal?

options.text: Cut her quotes by 10% on the next three bids
options.feedback: It acts fast on the stated reason. But if price wasn't the real cause, she gives away margin on every future deal and still loses.

options.text: Call the buyer in a week and ask what they chose instead and how they decided
options.feedback: It costs one awkward 15-minute call. In return she learns whether to fix her price, her offer, or nothing at all.

options.text: Send a gracious thank-you and put her energy into the next bids
options.feedback: It keeps the relationship warm and saves time. But she walks into the next three bids with the same blind spot.

cards.title: Price wasn't the reason.
body: Dana called ten days later. She didn't pitch. She asked what they did instead.

They had stayed with their old supplier. Her price was only about 4% higher. The real issue: her lead time was three weeks, and the old supplier delivered in one. The warehouse manager, whom Dana never met, worried about running out of boxes during the switch.
"Price" was simply the easiest thing to write in an email.

cards.title: Learning from lost deals
body: A **loss review** is a short, honest conversation with a customer who said no, aimed at learning why, not at winning them back.
The key idea: the stated reason is often the *polite* reason. Price is safe to name. It sounds objective and ends the conversation.
The real reason usually hides in two places: what the customer chose instead (including doing nothing), and the moment in the process where you quietly fell behind.

image.label: An iceberg: 'Price' above water, real reasons below
image.brief: 빙산 인포그래픽. 수면 위 작은 부분에 "Price". 수면 아래 큰 부분에 "Lead time", "Switching worry", "Someone you never met", "Doing nothing felt safer". 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Ask about what happened, not what they think.
body: Wait a week or two, so the decision feels finished. Promise no pitch, and keep it short. Then ask:
list: **What did you choose instead?** Another supplier, a workaround, or nothing
**When did we start falling behind?** The moment matters more than the verdict
**Who else weighed in?** Losses often come from people you never met
**What would have changed the outcome?** Listen for facts, not feelings
cards.callout: Write down their words, not your interpretation.

cards.title: One loss is a story. Five are a pattern.
body: A single conversation can mislead you. Keep a simple log: deal, stated reason, real reason, what they chose instead.
After a handful of losses, patterns appear. Maybe you keep losing to "do nothing", which means the problem doesn't feel urgent enough. Maybe you lose when one specific role joins late.
Ask winners too. Knowing why people said yes tells you what to protect.
cards.softwareNote: Digital products leave a trail. Before the call, check what the prospect actually did during the trial. Usage data shows where they stopped. The call tells you why.

cards.title: Don't let one loud loss steer the business.
body: Some buyers still won't tell you the truth, and some won't take the call at all. That's fine. Don't chase.
A detailed loss can feel more important than it is. One distributor wanting one-week delivery doesn't mean every customer does. Look for repeats before rebuilding your factory or product.
And never turn the call into a second pitch. The moment it feels like selling, the honesty stops.

cards.title: Now it's a booking app for clinics.
body: You sell scheduling software to small dental clinics. Three of your last five free trials ended without a purchase. All three said the same thing: "Not the right time for us."
What's your next move?

options.text: Build the reminder feature the last clinic mentioned
options.feedback: It feels like listening. But one comment isn't a pattern, and you might spend months on something that wasn't the reason.

options.text: Check each trial's usage, then ask each clinic what they're using now
options.feedback: You combine what they did with what they say. If all three stalled at importing their old calendar, you've found a fixable cause hiding behind "timing".

options.text: Accept it's about timing and follow up in six months
options.feedback: Polite and low-effort, and some clinics may return. But "not the right time" is often a soft no, and you learn nothing in the meantime.

cards.title: A lost deal is honest data, if you ask for it.
body: The first reason a customer gives is usually the easy one. Ask what they chose instead and where you fell behind.
**Try it today:** pick one deal you lost in the last three months. Send a short note asking for 15 minutes to learn, not to sell.
